style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Okay. Considerations for choosing a position.
Any position can get a top score. But some positions are much easier to explain. So let's see which ones.
We've already said that your opinion doesn't matter. You can hold whatever opinion you like.
Nobody lowers your score because you chose one opinion and not the other.
But, there are considerations for choosing a position. Some positions are better to choose, because they'll be much easier to explain.
Now, before we start, I want to make this clear. These are considerations, not instructions. You don't have to choose that position.
Sometimes some considerations will point one way, and others the other way... and you'll have to decide.
But they'll help you choose the position that's easier for you to explain.
The first one: material for arguments in the task.
We saw in the task analysis that we get suggestions for the main arguments of one side, of the other side, and so on.
So let's choose the side that has more detail. They're already giving me main arguments. So, let's use them.
I mean, why should I struggle to come up with arguments of my own?
The second one: your opinion.
If you hold a certain position, why? Explain why you think that. Something convinced you.
It's not like you tossed a coin. Heads, I support the cameras, tails, privacy. No. Something made you choose that position. So use it.
Explain why you think so. And that's exactly what we need to do in an argument essay.
So start from what you really think. But if the other side is much easier to explain, it's completely fine to switch. The raters score how well you argue, not what you believe.
The third one. In quite a few tasks, there's the common good against the good of the individual.
And usually, it's easier to explain the common good.
Take an offender in prison, for example. Here the common good is more important than the good of the individual. We take away the individual's freedom, to protect the public.
The fourth. Sometimes there's a moral consideration hiding somewhere in the task.
Then it'll usually be easier to explain the more moral position. Again, not always. But if there is one, it's easier.
For example, if there's a vulnerable group, a weak group, and I want to take its side to protect it, because it can't protect itself.
Compared with the other side, which can look after itself.
The fifth: changing the existing situation.
Usually the preference is not to change. If something already exists, it'll probably be easier to explain.

For example, a new law that people are talking about cancelling. Hmm, they only just passed it, and you already want to cancel it? If they passed it, there was probably some logic to it. And you can explain that logic.
But sometimes it's an old law they want to cancel. Then I need to think a bit, and not be so sure. Maybe the law is old, and the situation has changed, so it needs changing. Or maybe not.
And sometimes they want to pass a new law. Here too, I need to weigh it. Usually we'll prefer not to, because if the law doesn't exist, there's probably a reason it wasn't passed until now.
But again, these are only considerations.
The sixth: degree tasks. Don't choose the extremes.
When I choose an extreme in a degree task, it shows a lack of critical thinking. Like I'm not taking the other side into account. As if I don't even see it.
By the way, in Jewish law, you may have heard of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel. Shammai are the strict ones, they don't compromise. Hillel are the more moderate ones.
And which way does the law go? It follows Hillel. Because the world isn't black and white. There's grey. Lots of grey, in different shades.
So if I think to a great extent, I'm close to yes. If to a small extent, I'm close to no. But I try not to choose the ends.
Now, when there's an absolute end and a flexible end, like we saw before, I don't want the absolute end. I want the flexible one.
Like the name says, it gives me flexibility. It lets me present a complex position.
For example: should there be a period of exclusivity for a company that develops a new medicine?
On one hand, companies develop medicines, and they want to make a profit and get back what they invested. On the other hand, there are patients here. Human life is at risk.
If I say no, there's no exclusivity, then I've chosen the absolute end.
Usually I'd rather choose the flexible end. I can say yes, but only for a month. That's extreme, of course, but I can play with the range. A year, five years, ten years.
Or I give them exclusivity, but I require them to give the medicine for free when someone's life is in danger. So I have the whole range of the axis to choose from.
Now, a very important part of what we're assessed on is critical thinking. And how well we deal with opposing positions.
To understand that the other side has a point. That our side isn't completely right.
And here I want to talk about a complex position. It lets me have my cake and eat it.
I don't choose end A or end B. I choose side A, but I add a few reservations. Safeguards, that help solve some of the disadvantages I'd have if I went all the way with side A.
If you do it well, a complex position shows critical thinking. That you take the opposing view into account. That you understand nobody is simply right or wrong.
So in our camera task, I don't choose the absolute end, no cameras. I choose the flexible end, because it lets me present a complex position.
Yes, I do want face-recognition cameras in public spaces. But I understand the problem, the danger to privacy. So I want to add safeguards.
For example, a special body that handles the data, so fewer people get to see it. And information-security measures, so the database doesn't leak.
Now, a complex position needs a clear limit, one that comes from your reasons.
So, is it better? Well, a middle position is often easier to defend, so it can help you. But the raters don't give extra points for it. A clear one-sided essay can score just as high.
The seventh: human rights. Quite a few tasks have a clash between this right and that right.
And many students find it harder to explain a right when there's no detail about it.
If the task gives detail about the right, why it's a problem, what happens, then I have material for arguments.
Back to the cameras. Two rights, privacy and security. For security, there was detail. Prevent offences, stop them, catch offenders afterwards. Great. Lots of material.
For privacy, there's no detail. They just say it would seriously harm privacy. That's it.
And for many students, that's harder to explain. So for those students, it may be better to choose the right with detail, not the one without.
And sometimes, more rarely, there are three-opinion tasks. If you can, think about the middle. It's often the easiest to defend.
Why? Because the middle is a complex position. Not black, not white. Grey. If you do it well, it shows critical thinking.
When I choose one of the ends, it's as if I'm at a hundred and zero.
When I choose a complex position, it's as if I take eighty percent of the advantages of this side, and eighty percent of the advantages of that side.

Eighty from each side is a hundred and sixty together, compared with a hundred and zero. I don't keep the cake completely whole, but my position keeps more of the good on both sides. And that's what makes it easier to defend.
So let's go through our task, and see which considerations we have, and what they recommend.
Material for arguments: we have a lot, and it's for the cameras. The opponents just say it would harm privacy. No detail.
Our opinion: well, I don't know yours. Each of you has your own.
Common good against individual good: not here. In both cases it's the common good. We look after everyone's security, and everyone's privacy.
A moral consideration: I don't see anything special here.
Changing the existing situation: this one says against the cameras, because right now there's no such law, and no such cameras.
Degree: this one is for the cameras. Against is the absolute end. For lets me say yes, with reservations and safeguards.
And rights: for the cameras again, because the supporters' right, security, comes with detail. And privacy doesn't.
So that's the lesson on considerations for choosing a position. And just a reminder, they're considerations, not instructions.
If I had to pick the most useful one in practice, it's degree tasks. Don't choose the extremes. The flexible end is usually easier to defend.
It leaves you room for a complex position, with a clear limit.

And one more thing. The position you choose now is a first position. A leaning. After you find your arguments and test them, you confirm it... or you change it, if the other side turns out to be easier to explain.
